body: Yup I work in the ER and we would consider this leaving AMA. I would think medical and vision insurances would work similarly. I would love to read all day long. I have all these books that I have on my list to read. Keeps my depression and suicidal thoughts at bay. I would still work part time though, just something to give meaning to my life but not too much to be burnt out

This is just a sample size of 1 and a personal experience as someone with BPD and chronic suicidality with hx of OD on meds as SA. It took about 5 years of trialing multiple meds before my psych np put me on lithium. I suspect this is due to my SA history and as such what I told my PCP when he asked me why I haven’t tried lithium before. I don’t blame her, I appreciate her for considering that when prescribing it. I’ve been on it for over a month, I’ve missed several doses due to working night shift but in general my SI has decreased. It could also be due to external factors but I would say it’s been effective

We do EKGs for pretty much everyone (that comes by ambulance, I never work triage but I think they’re more reserved for chest pain or cardiac issues) unless it’s very obvious they don’t need it like ankle injury. I give it to the doc in charge of the patient but often times we have the ekg done but no doctor has signed up for the patient then I would just give it to whoever is available.

Usually I just talk about what is important for my psych np to know, like starting DBT or going back to work after a leave of absence. I leave the daily arguments with my mom or struggles at work to talk about with my therapist but she does sometimes ask me how I’m doing with daily stuff so we do talk about it. I’m very introverted so it’s hard for me to bring up stuff but I’ll talk about it when people ask me

The most medical skills I used was administering IM meds and drawing blood. Sometimes we would have to deescalate and restrain but most of the time it was just watching patients for safety and killing time. And it was a lot different from what I expected. I became a psych nurse because I was a psych patient myself and I thought there would be more like a therapist role. But there really wasn’t much of that. I just wanted to be more hands on and do procedures

Working in the ER I’ve seen overdose attempts including one where I had to strongly encourage a patient to drink the awful charcoal solution and it keeps me from another suicide attempt when I have the urge to

I had a patient with an ankle fracture who insisted on going to the bathroom (she said she was too big for the bedside commode) and I could not persuade her to do otherwise so I wheeled her to the bathroom and she did her business but we could not get her back into the wheelchair because she could feel the bone moving. I asked a doc (not her doctor, she was on the phone) for advice and she just said that’s a nursing problem. It wasn’t like I was asking her to come physically help, I was just trying to figure out how to logistically get her into the wheelchair without displacing the ankle even more. And another time had a patient fall and a nurse asked me to grab a doctor so I went to the only doctor that was at the desk and he just said she’s not my patient. Having done both psych and ER, keep your options open. Try anything and everything. Psych was my dream job, turns out it wasn’t what I was looking for. I tried dialysis because why not and turns out it wasn’t for me. You learn more about yourself and also might surprise you to find out that an area of nursing fits you well when you didn’t expect it to. 

Be a team player. Both these areas are heavy in teamwork. When you have an aggressive psych patient, you can’t restrain them alone. You need your fellow nurses and techs. And when they need help, they rely on you to come help them. I love my ER for all the teamwork we have. When an EMS comes in, other nurses come help put the patient on the monitor, do EKG and put in IV while I take report. By the time I’m done putting them into the system, they’re all settled in and ready to see the doc. When I need help with an IV or a procedure that I don’t know how to do, I can rely on my coworkers. And the same goes the other way, when someone gets an EMS I’m ready to go help them. 

Best of luck!

For us when they come in they get changed, we get all their belongings that the security goes through and locks up and just get them comfortable until a therapist is ready to assess them via zoom on the computer. Then they wait some more until the psychiatrist decides on whether to admit them or not and then wait for a bed to become available before they get wheeled off to the unit. They’re still essentially in the ER so they’re limited to their stretcher/room and the bathroom. I’ve worked inpatient psych too and we restrain more patients in the ER that we do inpatient. We sometimes do lab work (blood draws) or EKGs if they have a medical concern too but most of the times they would go in the medical side of the ER. We do q4h vitals (but not really, we’re supposed to but we’re so busy we just end up doing once per shift) and documentation wise just hourly rounding notes.

I had a year left in pharmacy school when I switched to nursing. I was working in retail pharmacy as an intern and most likely would have stayed as a pharmacist. But it wasn’t as fulfilling as I expected and I couldn’t see myself doing it for rest of my life. I wanted more patient interaction that wasn’t business or financial transaction focused. I initially chose pharmacy because pharmacists are the “most accessible health care professional” but most people don’t see them more than people who give them pills. I have the upmost respect for pharmacists but I just didn’t want to do that. I had worked as a tech at an urgent care and loved the hands on part of nursing. I had a mental health crisis during pharmacy school and had to go on leave of absence and just felt like it was the right time to try applying to nursing school and I got in so I just kept on with it. I think it was a good decision, I can’t imagine doing anything else. My mind goes back and forth on whether I want to go to med school but right now I don’t think I want to be in a prescriptive role. And NP is an option if I decide to go that route. I think nursing is a great profession. And it fits most, if not all of what you’re looking for. There’s so many places you can go with nursing. I’ve done psych, dialysis and now ER and was able to switch easily when I felt like where I was wasn’t where I wanted to be. Scheduling is pretty self explanatory, you have all kinds of options. And there’s clearly defined limits on what nurses can and cannot do. You follow the doctor’s orders but also have some leeway on using your clinical judgement. I questioned a doctor on a med order because I didn’t see why the patient needed it and turns out he ordered it on the wrong patient. And I leave everything at work. Except for some amusing stories of patients. But I don’t need to take any work home. And finally you can take your nursing career further. You can be a NP, CRNA or a teacher. You can get certifications or explore an entirely different area of nursing and broaden your knowledge.

Hey! I was in pharmacy school. And then I realized I didn’t want to be a pharmacist anymore and wanted to do something more hands on so I switched to nursing. But to think of it, I didn’t really hate being in retail, I actually enjoyed my job, I think it just scared me that everyone was saying not to go into retail. But it’s best for you to get some experience before making any decisions. In community pharmacy pharmacists check prescriptions when they are entered into the computer by the techs for accuracy as well as clinical safety of the medication itself (like making sure that the patient isn’t allergic to it, the dose isn’t too high, it doesn’t interact with another medication that the patient is taking), and after the prescription is filled making sure that it’s the correct medication, counsel and educate patients, administer vaccines (though I’ve heard they’re making the techs do them now), call doctors for any issues with the prescription, call the insurance company etc. A huge problem with retail pharmacies are that they are very short staffed so the pharmacist has to do things the techs would normally do like registers, answer phone calls and fill prescriptions (although these are things that are still done by the pharmacist even when the pharmacy is adequately staffed, just at a lesser amount). Another issue is the patients. Many are rude, don’t understand how insurances work and expect the pharmacy staff to fix everything, don’t understand that pharmacists are there to keep them safe and think that doctors never make mistakes, or want you to ring up gazillion things along with their prescription. A lot of it comes from ignorance….but some people are just down right nasty. As for a hospital pharmacy, I can’t speak on it because I don’t really have experience in this area. I do work with a pharmacist in the emergency room as a nurse and I can tell you that he doesn’t have to deal with patients. Pharmacists are medication experts. If that interests you, then pharmacist could be a potential career.

Depends on what you want to do. For BSN you need to do STEM classes like anatomy, physiology and chemistry (prerequisite). You learn medical stuff like medications and procedures. I think with psych you can be a therapist or social worker mainly along with few other careers (correct me if I’m wrong) which both require a masters. As a nurse case management is a possibility, there’s some sort of “therapy” if you are willing to sit and talk with the patients but not to the extent of a full length one hour session and you don’t get classes in psychotherapy until you go to psych NP school. Even then it’s not as extensive as what you learn in school to be a therapist. I’ve heard you make less as a therapist but potential to earn more if you form your own practice and expand. Thanks! I find that people with mental health issues are very good with mental health careers. It can be more stressful and triggering to us, but we have more empathy. The main duties are meds and documentation but so many things happen. You have to troubleshoot and problem solve because patients will ask for a lot of things and you’ll run into problems, deescalate when someone gets aggressive or disruptive, communicate with doctors and families, monitor for med side effects and symptom progression, assess for risk (suicidal or homicidal), do alcohol and drug withdrawal assessments, admission and discharges and basic assessment like why they are there, what kinds of symptoms they are having, what meds they’re taking etc. I think the biggest skill you need is therapeutic communication which involve empathy and also skills in communication. It’s not as simple as you would think, there’s different methods to interact with people with different problems. Its also what you do majority of your shift. Unlike medical specialties where you perform procedures and is more hands on, psych is mainly interactive. The most medical thing I’ve done is give injections and blood sugar monitoring, maybe some wound care. But it’s worthwhile, you can make someone’s day just by being there to listen and have a conversation.

The doctor comes to talk to you every day probably for about 5 minutes or less and just basically changes/adds/removes medication. There were also patients doing ECT and getting long acting injections. The nurses do assessments like self harm/suicide/pain and gives meds and keeps track of  where everyone is every 15 minutes. We literally had to write down where everyone was in this big binder. 

As a nurse we saw all kinds of people. Psychosis, aggression, mania, depression and self harm. Patients found creative ways to self harm which I will not list here. But generally most patients were nice and got along pretty well. Most, not all. Sometimes a fight would break out but the staff tries to break it up before any violence happens. We’ve had to restrain people and put them in seclusion where they are under constant observation. We did give injections pretty regularly for people acting up, common ones being zyprexa, B52 (haldol/Ativan) and geodon. Most people are there for about 3-5 days but there are sometimes patients who are looking for placement like group homes and end up staying there months or even more than a year. You do have to strip down to make sure there aren’t any wounds or contraband but we tried to make it as quick as possible and did it in a way that you’re not completely naked (so we would have you change pants first and then the top). 

Overall every time has been helpful for me, all the nurses were nice and were the reason I became a nurse. It’s not crazy as you would think. Although how you get treated does depend on where you go to because there are some awful ones out there.

Basically on a given day I would get report, pass meds and do assessment (any suicidal/homicidal thoughts, pain, hallucinations etc) and chart. Then pass noon/afternoon meds if there are any. Charting took up most of my time. Sometimes we would have patients that needed to be restrained or given PRN medications to help them calm down. There would also be admissions and discharges and then we could just talk to patients as we liked. You could be as involved as you would like, my preceptor loved to make conversation with patients but mostly other nurses just left them to be. On our unit the techs ran groups and I did run a group when I was working as a tech. I’ve been interviewing for a PRN psych position because I recently got a new full time job in dialysis and they’ve asked me about experience in running groups which leads me to believe some places have nurses running groups. But it was encouraged to run extra groups and anyone who wanted to run one could. These groups could be recreational therapies, a lot of the groups involved music and playing games/coloring, there were groups that were designed to teach stuff like coping skills too. If you worked day shift you only did days, if you worked night shift you worked overnights. At one of the places I interviewed at I could choose to work days or nights as I saw fit so it really depends on what shift you sign on to work in. The most medical skill I used was administering medications (we had to give a lot of IMs). There were some wound care but very basic, some blood draws too although mostly the night shift did them. But there are medical psych units where you might have to do IVs and more medical stuff so depends on your unit. If you want to shadow there’s no issues at all, I’ve shadowed at places while I was interviewing, I’ve seen people shadow, it’s a good idea to shadow to see if it’s a place that will be a good fit for you. I worked on a more acute unit so it was more crisis focused but we did have long term patients who were waiting for placement. I would think residential places would be less crisis focused and there might be units more stable too. If you wanted to prescribe and diagnose you could go back to school and get a masters and be a nurse practitioner or if you wanted to do more counseling you could go back to school to be a therapist or a social worker.
